name: Thymoquinone
short: Animal data: injected thymoquinone caused fetal loss in pregnant rats. It may be one cause of severe skin reactions to black seed oil (case series of 3). Lab data: possible warfarin interaction.
text: The only human trial of thymoquinone itself among the cited sources, a 90-day randomised study in 60 people with type 2 diabetes that added thymoquinone (50 or 100 mg a day) to metformin, set out to evaluate safety, but its abstract gives only blood glucose and HbA1c results and no safety results. Most other evidence is animal or laboratory data. In pregnant rats, a single intraperitoneal injection of 50 mg/kg on day 11 of gestation caused complete fetal resorption, and 46.2% of implants were resorbed when it was given on day 14, with no thymoquinone-related malformations in the surviving fetuses; 15 mg/kg was the no-observed-adverse-effect level, and the authors concluded that 35 and 50 mg/kg may disrupt embryonic development. In mice given thymoquinone by mouth, 100 mg/kg a day in a subacute study caused no deaths but did cause liver toxicity, with no observed adverse effects at 10 mg/kg a day. On the skin, a case series of three women with severe acute contact dermatitis from black seed oil (Nigella sativa oil), with more than 15% skin detachment and fever, named thymoquinone and p-cymene as possibly the main agents involved. For interactions, laboratory data only: thymoquinone inhibited warfarin metabolism in an enzyme study, and the authors predicted that more than 18 mg a day of thymoquinone, or more than 1 g a day of black seed or its oil, might alter warfarin pharmacokinetics; in another test-tube study it strongly inhibited CYP3A4 and moderately inhibited CYP2C19, and the authors said this may cause herb-drug interactions with medicines metabolised by these enzymes.
